answer.sourceLine: Chanel published the line — in French — among 31 aphorisms headed “Maximes et Sentences” in the Paris edition of Vogue for September 1938, page 57, as traced by Quote Investigator ↗. The English sentence people share is a translation of that maxim, not words Chanel wrote in English.

source.excerpt: Nos maisons sont nos prisons; sachons y retrouver la liberté dans la façon de les parer.
trail: Quote Investigator traced the maxim to “Maximes et Sentences” by Gabrielle Chanel in the September 1938 Vogue of Paris, page 57 ↗, printing the French original and noting that the statement appeared among 31 items in a two-page spread.

The magazine itself is documented: the Bibliothèque nationale de France catalogue record for Vogue (Paris) ↗ shows Condé Nast publishing the French edition from June 1920 onward — the run that includes the September 1938 issue.

A second, independent English rendering appears in Hal Vaughan’s biography Sleeping with the Enemy: Coco Chanel’s Secret War, published by Vintage ↗, which also links the maxims to Pierre Reverdy and to Chanel’s Riviera villa La Pausa.

A useful negative check: English Wikiquote’s Coco Chanel page ↗ has only “Quotes” and “Quotes about Chanel” as content sections and lists nothing about homes, prisons or decoration — so its silence is not a verdict against the line, merely a gap.
source.excerptNote: Chanel’s French, as transcribed by Quote Investigator from Vogue (Paris), September 1938, page 57. The English line in circulation — “Our homes are our prisons; let us find freedom in their decoration” — is QI’s translation of it; Hal Vaughan’s 2011 biography renders the same sentence “Our homes are our prisons; one finds liberty in their decoration.”

source.rightsNote: The maxim was first published in Vogue (Paris) for September 1938 — well after the 1931 line that marks the U.S. public domain — so both Chanel’s French text and the issue it appeared in are presumed still in copyright. The English sentence this page headlines is a separate, more recent work — the rendering Quote Investigator published on 18 December 2020, carrying its own rights; Hal Vaughan’s 2011 English version is a different derivative work with rights of its own. Nothing here should be treated as public domain.

author.name: Coco Chanel
author.heading: Who was Coco Chanel?
author.metaLine: 1883–1971 · French couturière, founder of the House of Chanel
author.bio: Gabrielle Bonheur “Coco” Chanel (19 August 1883 – 10 January 1971) was a French fashion designer and businesswoman who built the House of Chanel and, in the years after the First World War, made a sporty, pared-back ease into the reigning standard of feminine style. She wrote very little for publication, which is part of why a signed Chanel text like the 1938 “Maximes et Sentences” matters: most of the lines the internet hangs on her come secondhand, from biographers and interviewers. Her couture house closed in 1939 at the outbreak of war and she did not reopen it until 1954, after years in Switzerland and an unresolved wartime record of collaboration.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: Coco Chanel is one of the internet’s great fake-quote magnets, so the reflex is to assume this one is invented too. It isn’t — but almost everything around it gets muddled: the language it was written in, who helped write it, and where it can be found.

items.why: Chanel wrote in French. Quote Investigator gives “let us find freedom in their decoration” and records Hal Vaughan’s “one finds liberty in their decoration” ↗, noting the saying can be rendered several ways. Neither is a Chanel sentence in English — quoting either as her exact words overstates the case.

Quote Investigator quotes Vaughan’s 2011 biography saying Reverdy — the poet, and Chanel’s lover — “helped Chanel compile a series of maxims that would years later be published in Vogue” ↗. Chanel published them under her own name, and QI concludes the piece is hers, but the hand behind the polish may not have been hers alone.

items.who: Décor blogs, Pinterest boards and quote aggregators
items.why: The line circulates in English with no publication attached, which is exactly how fabricated Chanel quotes travel. It doesn’t help that Wikiquote’s Chanel page carries no maxim about homes, prisons or decoration ↗ — so the obvious place to check comes back empty, and the real one looks fake.

misattribution.truthLine: It is genuine Chanel, and it has an address: “Maximes et Sentences,” Vogue (Paris), September 1938, page 57 — one of 31 maxims, located and transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it landed
lead: “Maximes et Sentences” was a two-page spread in the Paris Vogue of September 1938: 31 short epigrams signed by Gabrielle Chanel, per Quote Investigator’s citation of page 57 ↗. It was not dress advice. It was a couturière trying her hand at the French moralist tradition — the aphorism as a form — and the home maxim is a small piece of sleight of hand: it concedes that a house shuts you in, then hands the confinement straight back to you as a medium.

The timing gives it an edge nobody planned. Chanel closed her couture house the following year at the outbreak of the Second World War ↗ and did not reopen it until 1954. The line also found a second life in 2020, when readers under lockdown went looking for the French original — which is the request that prompted the Quote Investigator inquiry in the first place.
context.detailsSummary: One French original, two English versions
detailsBody: Chanel wrote “Nos maisons sont nos prisons; sachons y retrouver la liberté dans la façon de les parer.” The second clause is loose enough that translators reasonably diverge: la façon de les parer is nearer “the way we adorn them” than “decoration” in the interior-design sense, and sachons is a first-person-plural imperative — roughly “let us learn how to.”

Quote Investigator offers “Our homes are our prisons; let us find freedom in their decoration” and notes Hal Vaughan’s alternative, “Our homes are our prisons; one finds liberty in their decoration” ↗, adding that the saying “can be translated into English in several different ways.” Neither English form is Chanel’s; both are honest renderings of the same French.

sourcesVerified.claim: The French original is "Nos maisons sont nos prisons; sachons y retrouver la liberté dans la façon de les parer," published in "Maximes et Sentences" by Gabrielle Chanel in Vogue (Paris), September 1938, page 57, among 31 items; QI's English rendering is "Our homes are our prisons; let us find freedom in their decoration"; Hal Vaughan's 2011 book gives "one finds liberty in their decoration" and says Reverdy helped Chanel compile the maxims at La Pausa.
The BnF catalogue record describes Vogue (Paris), published by Condé Nast in Paris, running from June 1920 onward.

English Wikiquote's Coco Chanel page contains only 'Quotes' and 'Quotes about Chanel' as content sections (its third level-2 heading is 'External links') and no quotation containing 'prison', 'decorat', 'home', 'house' or 'maison'.

Gabrielle Bonheur 'Coco' Chanel lived 19 August 1883 – 10 January 1971; her couture house closed in 1939 with the outbreak of World War II and she returned to Paris in 1954 to revive her fashion house.
Sleeping with the Enemy: Coco Chanel's Secret War is by Hal Vaughan, published by the Vintage imprint.
Pierre Reverdy (13 September 1889 – 17 June 1960) was a French poet associated with Surrealism, Dadaism and Cubism.
